#99407. Tech Report: History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2577 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary.
  • The upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game.
  • It's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary. After years of long-shot competition against companies with vastly more significant resources, American Motors Corporation won the Trans-Am championship. The following year, it did it again.

The upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game. Yet, not long after the metaphorical credits would have rolled following that fairytale ending, the car responsible for those victories would be no more. The car was the AMC Javelin, and by the end of 1974, it was gone.

It's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history. The icons become institutions, celebrated and remixed into anniversary editions, nostalgic ad campaigns, and generations of increasingly expensive collectibles. Everything else is a footnote.

Recent findings suggest that but the Javelin's existence has more to say than the handful of years in which it was made, as its brief run coincided remarkably with a transformative shift in the broader history of the automobile in the United States. It arrived in 1968, when American prosperity seemed limitless, and disappeared just as the country was beginning to confront the limits of that optimism.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, the Javelin became something its creators could have scarcely imagined. Its story is one of ambition, ingenuity, and the kind of underdog triumph that's impossible not to root for. Except, it's also about the difference between reaching a dream and being able to hang onto it.

In the early '60s, the American automobile was clearly becoming more than just a way to get around. The baby boomers were getting old enough to drive, and cars weren't just for families anymore. Women took to the road in increasing numbers, and multi-car households became more common. As a growing market with more disposable income revealed an appetite for cars that were more fun and even had a little personality, carmakers were eager to oblige.

According to recent reports, ford led the way. The company introduced the Mustang at the New York World's Fair on April 17, 1964. The Mustang had a long hood and short rear deck that fundamentally changed the posture of what a fun car could be and started at just $2,368. Available options and configurations could accommodate buyers interested in anything from a free-spirited runabout to a serious performance car.

Ford expected to sell 100,000 Mustangs a year. It took 22,000 orders on the first day, and first-year sales exceeded 400,000 cars. The era of the American pony car had arrived, but that meant more than just the Mustang.

Plymouth had actually beaten Ford to market with the Barracuda, but Ford gets the credit for turning the segment into a sensation. Chevy answered with the Camaro, Pontiac arrived with the Firebird, and the Mercury-branded Cougar followed its Ford sibling into production.

In a recent development, the pony car offered buyers individuality, excitement, and an invitation to have fun with cars in ways that went beyond simply buying a family sedan with a needlessly-large V8. American Motors didn't have one.

American Motors Corporation built a reputation around economical, everyday cars since the company was established by a merger of the Nash-Kelvinator Corporation and the Hudson Motor Car Company, which, in 1954, represented the largest merger in United States history. As America embraced the fun, upcoming Mustang and its early pony car contemporaries, AMC was struggling with a stodgy and decidedly unexciting reputation.

Enter the 1968 Javelin, a sporty coupe developed under AMC design chief Richard Teague after he had personally advocated for AMC to get in on the pony car segment and start shaking off the buttoned-down, no-fun image. The car had a long hood and daring proportions that clearly made a play at the burgeoning market without being a copy of any that existed so far. In-period advertising called out the Mustang by name, leaning into the rivalry and calling out the Javelin's differentiating features like large, contoured bumpers, hand-finished roof joints, and extra room inside.

Underpinning what some would say is one of the most attractive muscle cars ever forgotten was the basic architecture of AMC's Rambler American, a car that was explicitly built to minimize operating costs and compete with the rise of economical imports. Yet, AMC was able to take the bones of one of the least exciting vehicles on the road at the time and use it as a jumping-off point that could do more than turn heads. Engine choices included a 232-cubic-inch inline-6, 290 and 343 V8s, and, eventually, a 390-cubic-inch V8 producing 315 gross horsepower. A 390-powered Javelin SST tested by Car and Driver reached 60 mph in 6.9 seconds.

Sources indicate that people noticed. AMC had first set out to sell just 35,000 Javelins but ended up building more than 50,000 in that first year.

The Mustang might have been leading the herd when it came to pony cars, but AMC wasn't content to spend the Javelin's existence playing catch up and running ads touting its superior headroom or trunk space. Even if the firm couldn't compete with Detroit's marketing or development budgets, it could at least try to out weird the competition.

Industry observers note that for 1969, AMC introduced its "Big Bad" paint colors: Big Bad Blue, Big Bad Green, and Big Bad Orange. These were absolutely eye-piercing finishes that came with body-colored bumpers and complementary hardware options like (fake) exhaust shields, stainless steel trim, and a roof-mounted spoiler. Unlike almost everything AMC had produced up until that time, subtlety was not part of the package (and it remains one of the classic coupes that looks sick with window louvers).

It has been revealed that in 1970, the organization doubled down, with 100 Javelin SSTs built as replicas of the cars in the Trans-Am racing series, finished in the over-the-top red, white, and blue livery of AMC's competition cars. There was not a unique high-performance engine under the hood, and the replicas came with the same 390-cubic-inch V8 available on the SST. So, aside from a ram-air hood and performance-oriented gearing, this was a car that was all about appearances.

That appearance was spectacular to be sure, though some of those 100 Trans-Am replicas ended up being repainted back into submission, presumably because drivers were getting more attention on the street than they bargained for. All that said, AMC saw that the Javelin had the potential to be a lot more than just a pony car dressed up like a race car. It was headed to the races, and the organization had every intention of winning.

It has been revealed that of course, there's a difference between having the willingness to sell customers a replica race car from the factory and actually competing on the track. Perhaps the likes of Ford and Chevrolet represented immovable racing incumbents, but AMC wasn't going to concede the point.

Recent findings suggest that in 1967, the company commissioned Ronnie Kaplan Engineering to prepare a handful of Javelins for the Sports Car Club of America's Trans-Am series, which included Mustangs and Camaros backed by Big Three resources and some of the best drivers in the world. The Javelins were powered by modified versions of AMC's existing V8s, bored out from a factory-stock 290-cubic-inches up to just over 304, but they were still no match for the competition in a straight line.

Despite the horsepower handicap, drivers Pete Revson and George Follmer drove AMC to six second-place finishes and landed third overall in the 1968 manufacturers' championship. It was a promising start, but the team remained a distant third behind the two well-funded factory-backed teams of Chevy and Ford. The following year, Kaplan's team failed to maintain the momentum and the series was roundly dominated by Penske Racing and its driver, Mark Donohue, driving for Chevrolet.

AMC had demonstrated that it could compete on the racetrack, but the little red, white, and blue Javelin had gone two seasons without a victory. It would have to do something differently if the company wanted a real shot at beating Ford and Chevy at their own game.

Sources indicate that penske and Donohue were two people who had just spent consecutive racing seasons beating up on AMC and its Javelin, but it turns out that they were also something else: free agents. Fresh off of delivering back-to-back manufacturers' championships for Chevrolet, the pair agreed to revise loyalties and see what they could do with the upstart Javelin. Donohue was anything but a mere hotshot racing driver. He had studied engineering at Brown University, and in addition to being behind the wheel, he was also team manager and chief engineer. Together, Penske and Donohue took to the engineering side of the problem first, starting out by questioning the Javelin's bored-out V8. What if instead of stretching AMC's 290 to the limit, they started with the organization's newer 360 V8, reducing its stroke to meet the series' displacement limit while producing enough horsepower to challenge Chevrolet?

Winning is what happened. Donohue drove the Javelin to the car's first three first-place finishes in 1970, and, for the first time, AMC managed to pick off one of its two massive factory rivals, pushing past Chevrolet and finishing second behind Ford. The Javelin wasn't just an oddball outsider hoping to deliver the occasional upset to establishment rivals. It was a serious car capable of winning against the best Detroit had to offer.

Of course, while Donohue and Penske were out winning races, AMC also had to continue being a manufacturer that makes and sells cars. For 1971, AMC released a substantially redesigned Javelin that was longer, lower, wider, and more visually striking. Bulging front fenders caught the public's eye, not to mention that of Donohue, who appreciated the breathing room the latest design would give to race tires on his Trans-Am cars.

Industry observers note that it was here that the AMC AMX shifted from its previous status as its own model in the AMC lineup, becoming a trim package for the up-and-coming Javelin. This new Javelin AMX could then be equipped with AMC's 401-cubic-inch V8, rated at 330 gross horsepower. And yet, somehow, this was just the beginning. The following year, AMC tapped fashion designer Pierre Cardin for an outrageous aesthetic overhaul that included colorful stripes taking over the interior, and, indeed, what was once the most conservative automaker was now creating the wildest muscle car graphics in the business. Along the way it built one of the era's automotive special editions that was truly special.

Industry observers note that people were taking notice, including the Alabama State Police, which placed an order for 100 of the 401-powered Javelins for use as cruisers. The Javelin had finally helped AMC shrug off its dull reputation as the company that brought America the Rambler.

Industry observers note that in 1971, American Motors finally reached the goal it'd been chasing since the Javelin started racing. Mark Donohue won seven of that season's 10 Trans-Am races and delivered AMC's first manufacturers' championship. The organization that had gotten its start building painfully sensible transportation had finally conquered one of America's most prestigious racing series. The following year, Roy Woods Racing took over the AMC effort, with George Follmer winning four races, becoming the first officially recognized driver's champion of the series, and bringing home the manufacturers' championship for a second time.

Recent findings suggest that after four straight years of throwing the Javelin squarely at the fiercest competition of the day, AMC had done it. But even so, this previously unthinkable victory came at a time when the foundation of the Trans-Am series was beginning to shift. Other manufacturers, Ford and Chevy included, had withdrawn factory support for the Trans-Am series the year before. They were still on the racetrack, but without the intense backing that had pushed the teams forward through previous seasons. Still, AMC was up against some of the fastest cars that the most formidable manufacturers had fielded the previous season, and some of the private teams were anything but amateurs -– it was the private Penske team that brought Chevrolet those back-to-back championships in the first place, after all.

The Javelin had reached the top. A team of engineers, drivers, and ambitious manufacturer people had turned the unlikely descendant of the Rambler into a championship-winning machine. The achievement was nothing short of extraordinary, only it happened just as the mountain was beginning to empty.

According to recent reports, the Javelin came of age in an America where the future seemed limitless, with more horsepower, unimaginable freedom, and an endless supply of cheap gasoline to keep it all roaring forward. But while the Javelin was winning car races and AMC was experimenting with wild paint colors plus Pierre Cardin aesthetics, the country itself was starting to feel different.

In a recent development, the Clean Air Act of 1970 introduced ambitious fresh emissions requirements, effectively tapping the brakes on what made the pony car segment sing. In '73 the oil embargo sent petroleum prices through the roof, and Americans who had never given a thought to a seemingly bottomless supply of oil  were suddenly weighing what they were going to do if gas ran out. The era of giant V8s drinking fuel right from the tap with no concern for tomorrow was coming to an end.

It has been revealed that the extraordinary irony for AMC was that the boring, practical reputation it had worked so hard to overcome was exactly what the market was starting to demand. Sensible, economical transportation was back in style, and despite years of running the other direction with the Javelin, the firm was well-positioned to capitalize on the shift, with cars like the Gremlin and the Hornet ready to meet the moment. AMC had finally built a performance champion, but its greatest opportunities lay in leaving it behind.

Sources indicate that in 1971, the Javelin was taking its victory lap on the national stage. Just three years later, it would be offered for the last time. 1974 marked the end of AMC's unlikely hero, leaving incumbent mainstays like the Mustang, Camaro, and Firebird to carry the segment forward into uncertain times.

AMC could have stayed in the game, navigating the fresh landscape as rivals were attempting, but the Javelin would have required significant updates to meet 1975 safety regulations, including an estimated $12 million investment in bumpers alone. The time had come to move on.

That following year, Mark Donohue crashed while practicing for the Austrian Grand Prix. He had seen the potential in AMC's alternative pony car, joining the team to both engineer it into contention and to sit behind the wheel. Donohue died following emergency brain surgery after the wreck, and so 1975 marked the loss of both the Javelin itself and an icon who was central to what it had become.

AMC had done what it set out to do. It had built a car exciting enough for the times, challenged the biggest carmakers in the country, and won it all, twice. Yet, after all that, it would turn out that what America needed just then wasn't a better Mustang after all. It needed a better Rambler.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating new multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

Autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

It has been revealed that the Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the tech giant has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”.

Recent findings suggest that drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

Sources indicate that speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”.

It has been revealed that or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

In a recent development, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at new energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

Industry observers note that the US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

It has been revealed that the latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the company consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

Sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the organization revealed an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

Sources indicate that “The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

Recent findings suggest that that’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

Photo: The vehicle electrification movement is far from over in the US, with the startup Aptera among the stakeholders betting on an EV sales rebound in the coming years (cropped, courtesy of Aptera).

In a recent development, another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning consumers after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

According to recent reports, the warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

Industry observers note that so what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

In a recent development, etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are at the moment investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In….

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal customers’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

Recent findings suggest that but Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Recent findings suggest that optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and remarked it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

It has been revealed that the uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Industry observers note that lighter remarked its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

It has been revealed that another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

Industry observers note that these incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

According to recent reports, traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank mentioned customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

It has been revealed that deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Industry observers note that crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

In a recent development, neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Industry observers note that crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

Toyota makes a whole lot of different cars. I want to hear what your favorite hypothetical GRMN silk purse from a base model sow's ear might be. Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University.
  • According to recent reports, she told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology.
  • According to recent reports, last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the organization, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University. It safe to say she knows a thing or two about computer technology and AI.

According to recent reports, she told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave new technology. Her concerns are spurred by the number of high profile computer engineers who have quit recently over fears that AI development is out of control.

According to recent reports, last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the organization, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology. The month before that, a researcher at Anthropic — which went public yesterday at a valuation $1.8 trillion dollars — warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”.

It has been revealed that “When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave,” Ferreras remarked. “it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely. We cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.”.

Ferreras warned that governments think of AI either as a “consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. Corporate lobbyists encourage this view as a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.

According to recent reports, “This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product. It is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives,” she said.

Sources indicate that interestingly, Michael Connolly, the award winning author of the Bosch and Lincoln Lawyer novels, published a book last year in which the family of a young woman, who was murdered by her boyfriend after he interacted with an AI agent, sues the company behind the AI agent. The essence of the lawsuit is that AI only does what it is programmed to do, and since the lead programmer of this particular AI agent was a misogynist in real life, it reflected his values when it interacted with humans. The book is called The Proving Ground and it is a fascinating read.

According to recent reports, while Ferreras applauds those who warn of the malignancies built into AI, she pointed out that humans have short attention spans. “Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. As a society, we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle — and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal. As the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.”.

In a recent development, in a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed, Ferreras told The Guardian. “Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labor investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI ‘from the outside,’ we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.”.

Recent findings suggest that an analogy can be made to the Federal Communications Commission, which licenses broadcasters and promotes the free flow of information to the public. The digital world thinks such controls are archaic, but the lack of them is a clear and present danger to a civil society.

Sources indicate that ferreras suggested that “governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistle blower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches, and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.”.

In addition, she argued that “legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.”.

Lastly, she supported the democratization of boardrooms and rewarding firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. “Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labor.” Some, like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, would characterize her suggestions as liberal claptrap, and they would be correct. Ferreras would happily unravel the “tech bro” manosphere in order to promote a more open and just society.

She pointed to the research by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, which demonstrates that technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity. Instead, institutions decide who benefits and who pays.

“Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls ‘democratic reason’ — the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making,” Ferreras wrote.

“Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and alignment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.”.

It has been revealed that ferreras’ point of view is decidedly liberal, and yet her arguments are clear and concise. How can we give so much power to digital agents and not take reasonable steps to ensure the needs of society as a whole are respected? The tech industry enjoys almost unfettered freedom of action today. It may be time to consider whether that is a good long term strategy.

Why Cars Need To Be Driven To Stay In Peak Condition

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

It has been revealed that humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us. Much like neglecting to stretch those hammies can add strain to certain movements, leaving your car untouched can cause components to seize up, and both can be a major pain in the butt. While time comes for us all and everything will eventually deteriorate from age, keeping active can still help keep us in peak shape and prevent additional challenges from arising.

Of course, life happens and sometimes that extra project car that you're "definitely going to have running next week" sits for weeks, months, or even years. However, this can have real consequences. Leaving your car stationary too long can result in brake corrosion, battery problems, fuel system challenges, and leaks. All can lead to reduced performance or potentially costly repairs.

Thankfully, many of these problems can be mitigated by simply using your vehicle for what it is designed for — regular driving! Taking a weekly cruise that lasts about 20 to 30 minutes, per AAA guidance, will help keep your vehicle's fluids flowing, parts lubricated, and battery charged. Turns out, hitting those favorite back roads is actually good for both you and your car.

It has been revealed that so what does regular driving help prevent? Well, in as little as a day or two, a thin layer of rust can form on the brake rotors of a parked car. Fortunately, this is mostly cosmetic and normal driving clears this up after a few stops, but over extended periods of time corrosion can set in and seize up braking components.

It has been revealed that fuel that sits in your gas tank lasts about three to six months before it starts to break down. In older cars with metal fuel tanks, condensation can collect and start to rust the tank out from the inside. Aged fuel and moisture in your fuel system can lower octane, gum up fuel injectors, and lead to reduced performance. Keeping your fuel tank full (in this economy?) and cycled through every few months will help mitigate fuel system issues.

It has been revealed that an glitch that may require immediate intervention is a weak crank or no start from a dead battery. Batteries naturally lose charge with time, and even more so depending on battery age or if there are any parasites drawing current when the vehicle is off. Additionally, cold weather reduces a battery's cranking power on top of the natural battery discharge. Routine driving helps keep your battery topped off via the alternator so your car is ready.

Sources indicate that tires and belts will eventually need replacing. You may even find a flat spot in a tire that's sitting for too long. Seals and gaskets that keep fluids in place can dry up and crack when not driven enough to keep everything conditioned, soft, and flexible, which can cause leaks throughout your vehicle's powertrain. Depending on the seal and severity of the leak, this may require repair and keep your vehicle stationary even longer.

In a recent development, if you know your car is going to be sitting for a while, there are a few steps you can take to protect your car. I grew up in the Northeast, where it's common to put away the "nice" car for a few months over the winter so it doesn't get destroyed by road salt. Indoor storage is optimal for protection from the elements, but I'm no Rockefeller and my cars get parked outside.

According to recent reports, the annual ritual involves topping off the tank and adding a fuel stabilizer to prevent fuel degradation. Attaching a trickle charger keeps a low current fed to the battery and helps it stay ready to go. Changing the oil prior to storage will remove contaminants from the engine as an added layer of protection. A good cleaning inside and out can keep blemishes or stains from setting in. With that prep out of the way, you should be safe to get through the season.

Industry observers note that when the time comes to start your car after it has been sitting for a while, do a quick visual inspection. Check for underinflated or flat tires, the presence of animals, and any new leaks. If the tires are okay, fluids are at normal levels, there aren't any pools below your car or new inhabitants, and your battery isn't dead, you should be good to go. Drive it easy until the engine comes up to temp and listen for any new or unusual sounds. Just like humans, keeping your car in peak shape requires attention. Doing so will keep both you and your car happier and healthier for many more miles.

Jay Leno Outlined The Largest Problem With Sports Car Makers Chasing High-End Buyers

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While many Americans are struggling to meet their basic needs, automakers are moving further upmarket. Porsche's mid-engined Mission S supercar concept, for example, is aimed at an ultra-wealthy clientele, with an estimated $500,000 starting price for the production model. And Jay Leno has something to say about this.

During an interview with TBPN on YouTube, Leno noted Porsche was "moving upscale" with the Mission S: "They want to be like Ferrari. Sell fewer cars [for] more money to fewer people." In the old days, he said, "A Ferrari had 800 miles and Porsche had 60,000. A Corvette, same thing." And back then, when people used to hold shootouts to find out which car was the fastest, "the only ones that indicated up would be Corvette and Porsche. Everybody else just didn't." Nowadays, Leno continued, people "buy a GT3 and [say,] 'I'm putting it away.'" He added, "Porsches have always been expensive, but they're not rare. There's a lot of them around.".

And while Leno mentions how someone reasonably financially successful could still aspire to own a Corvette, the lineup has gone fairly upmarket, especially with the ZR1X in the mix — although the ZR1X's starting price of roughly $230,000 is considerably lower than those of most modern Ferraris and Lamborghinis, it's still a pretty expensive automobile.

Leno concluded that this strategy of selling fewer but pricier cars is spreading across the auto industry and, more broadly, the economy as a whole. "You're either Motel 6 or the Four Seasons. ... We have no middle class anymore. And that's the sad thing.".

There's no official definition of the middle class, at least not one that's widely agreed upon. The Pew Research Center defines middle-income households as those with an income (adjusted for household size) that's between two-thirds and double that of the U.S. median household income. Upper-income households earn more than double the median, while lower-income households earn less than two-thirds of it. By that measure, 61% of Americans were part of the middle class in 1971, with that share dropping to 51% by 2023.

In fact, the share of household income held by the middle class has fallen in almost every decade since 1970. Middle-income households held 62% of all U.S. household income in 1970, but just 43% in 2022. Upper-income households, meanwhile, saw a massive gain in their share, jumping from 29% to 48%.

Industry observers note that the middle-class decline can also be attributed to the pace at which income grew. Inflation-adjusted incomes across all tiers improved between 1970 and 2022, but not at the same rate. Upper-income households saw 78% growth, compared with just 60% for middle-income households. Lower-income folks saw the least growth (55%). In 2024, the median income of an upper-income household was $278,800, versus $115,900 for middle-income and $38,400 for lower-income households, according to Pew's 2026 report. And while upper-income households had 6.8 times the typical income of lower-income households in 2001, that number had risen to 7.3 by 2024.

Industry observers note that it's deeply concerning how new car sales are booming for the rich and falling for everyone else. Some of our readers have shared how their finances are holding them back from buying a new car in 2026, and they are certainly not alone.

Perhaps Jay's take on the middle class being nonexistent is a bit of a stretch. But as you can tell, income inequality is real. According to the Economic Policy Institute, between 1979 and 2023, the average annual earnings of the bottom 90% of workers saw cumulative growth of 44%, while the top 0.1% posted staggering growth of 354%. Although Americans earning an hourly wage were getting bigger paychecks than in the '70s, their purchasing power had remained largely unchanged after you factor in inflation, per a 2018 study from Pew. And according to data gathered by Statista, average real wages were down 0.8% in July 2026 compared with January 2021.

According to recent reports, no wonder there's an affordability crisis. The data reveals that President Trump's repeated claims of it being "fake" and a "hoax" couldn't be further from the truth, and plenty of working families can attest to that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elle and Dakota Fanning have been in the spotlight for decades, but their upcoming project, “The Nightingale,” marks the first time they’ve played sisters onscreen—an experience that brought them “closer” together, both on set and at home.

While they’ve visited each other on set in the past and even separately played different versions of the same character in the 2001 film “I Am Sam,” Elle, 28, told Vanity Fair that actually working with each other is a totally different ball game.

It has been revealed that “It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer,” she remarked. “Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”.

Dakota, 32, confirmed that they took their mother’s advice.

“We did really savor it,” she stated. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything. That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”.

Industry observers note that that stated, the job wasn’t easy. The Fannings traveled to Budapest to shoot on location, where they lived together.

Sources indicate that “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” said Elle.

After a long day of using lots of “brain power” on set, the sisters had to find a way to “recharge” each evening.

For Dakota and Elle, that meant eating lots of Thai food and streaming “The Real Housewives,” true crime, and “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”—the TV series the younger sister stars in, which was released while they filmed “The Nightingale.”.

Dakota revealed that on a day off, she’d often find herself cleaning up after Elle, which was poetic as her character, Vianne, also tidies her sister Isabelle’s mess.

Recent findings suggest that “Her bed in the mornings is like a tornado has run through it,” she said. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”.

The older sister remarked that “it became a routine,” and she “always made her bed like that” when possible.

Elle said, “It’s art imitating life, because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed, too.”.

Dakota and Elle were born in Conyers, GA. As young girls, they traveled between the Atlanta suburb and Los Angeles to work before relocating to the West Coast full time.

“When we were younger, we wanted to make sure that people saw us differently, and we wanted to give each other space to carve our own path,” Elle told Vanity Fair in 2025. “But as adults, it’s been very fulfilling to merge.”.

One of the most major ways the sisters have merged their lives in adulthood was in 2017, when they purchased a gorgeous $2.3 million property together.

According to Architectural Digest, they lived in a Cape Cod-style home in the Valley Village area of San Fernando Valley.

The 4,550-square-foot residence was perched at the end of a private, gated driveway and had a very classic aesthetic with white rose bushes planted along the front walkway.

The interiors were defined by delicate details, such as baby blue brocade-patterned walls, intricate chandeliers, and coffered ceilings.

The sisters sold the six-bedroom, six-bathroom estate for just under $2.7 million in May 2020.

It’s clear that Dakota was a fan of the dwelling’s traditional style, as she bought a very similar-looking home in Toluca Lake for $2.95 million in 2019, just before offloading the property she shared with Elle.

Sources indicate that according to Architectural Digest, Dakota’s newer home spans 4,428 square feet and boasts five bedrooms and six bathrooms. It’s flooded with natural light and, like the first home, has crystal chandeliers, a pool in the backyard, and a double-height entry hall.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s no longer a chip problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:21 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

It has been revealed that as artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens swiftly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

According to recent reports, “It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava said. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”.

Srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

In a recent development, stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a latest tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava stated.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava stated.

Pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

Recent findings suggest that “For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava remarked.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

“So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava mentioned. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy.
  • Various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways.
  • Industry observers note that the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy. However, they're not always easy to understand. When a picture is worth a thousand words, deciphering signage with diagonal black-and-yellow stripes or arrows pointing in opposite directions is akin to playing Pictionary with toddlers: what is that shape supposed to mean?! Adding a few words can create even more ambiguity, like Pennsylvania's contribution to the worst road signs list. Which brings us to the narrows.

Various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways. The self-explanatory ones are emblazoned with the phrases "road narrows" and "narrow bridge." Less informative is the pictorial variation featuring an hourglass-like outline that may or may not be accompanied by vertical dashes down the middle — the figure's "hips" reference the road narrowing. Regardless of which version you see, the rules of engagement remain the same: proceed with caution.

Industry observers note that the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S. DOT's Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), sets the standards for all traffic-flow-related communications, including road markings, signs, and signals. Per the MUTCD, Road Narrows signs are part of the W5 series, which includes cautions for underpasses. Standardized to be yellow, warning signs will vary in shape. For the W5s, the MUTCD settled on a diamond.

You'll also find them only in specific places. Plenty of driving lanes narrow and widen, but only when the path is shrunk to a certain width will you come across a W5 sign. The exception is low-volume local streets with speed limits of 30 mph or less. At those speeds, you're likely able to see oncoming traffic.

According to recent reports, according to the MUTCD, a road's width must diminish so abruptly and sharply that opposing traffic cannot simultaneously pass at posted speed limits. For bridges, culverts, and underpasses, warnings are issued following the surface-street rules, as well as when the two-way road's clearance is 16 to 18 feet across. This measurement includes the shoulder, if there is one.

The guidance suggests warnings be posted roughly 155 to 325 feet ahead of narrowings in 25 mph sections and up to 990 feet in 55 mph sectors. If visibility is impaired due to curves or grades, those distances can be adjusted. In construction zones, especially dangerous highway work, the W5s switch to work-zone orange and should appear prior to lane tapers, while a second reminder can be placed closer to the work area.

Sources indicate that so, what should you do when you see a narrows sign? Because it's not a road closure and the number of lanes can be unchanged, you simply continue on. Just keep your vehicle centered and take things slow and easy, especially if there's oncoming traffic. If a large vehicle approaches, like a bus or truck, consider yielding and letting it through. Room to pass will be limited, even if there is a shoulder.

Sources indicate that on bridges, stick to your side of the road, reduce your speed, and definitely watch out for outside mirrors. If the bridge is too narrow for two vehicles, the rule of thumb is whoever arrives first gets dibs. If there's no room, there's no point in forcing your way through. Although these signs don't say how long the road narrows, the early heads-up gives you time to prepare.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van.
  • According to recent reports, inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner.
  • In a recent development, julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van. Our brief takeaway: “Kool like a Kia.” Should keep the bean counters happy.

According to recent reports, inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner. We hoped to check out the LDV eDeliver 5 van, touted as selling for under AU$50,000. However, there was no stock to view and we ended up chatting to the dealer and then moving on to the MG U9 BEV ute. You can read about it here. And then we found the Kia PV5 delivery van.

In a recent development, julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change. Since its launch in May, 496 PV5 have sold in Australia.

Recent findings suggest that the Kia PV5 reminded me a lot of the Renault Kangoo in both size and shape, and it is able to carry about the same payload. And the front looked like the BMW i3. The one we looked at had been sold and was awaiting a fitout as a camper van. The Norris Group Kia specialist was generous with his time and the information he shared. He has been selling the Kia EV5 for the past 5 months and delivered 5 of the vans. He sold his first one within a week of its arrival on the lot — to Ray, a driver working for Amazon.

In a recent development, ray appreciated the 390 km range. My friendly sales rep tells me that this will be increased in 2027 models to 420 km. Ray was getting out of diesel and most of his questions were around charging and regen braking. Most of his trips were around the burbs and he was not intending to take the van on the highway. The Kia PV5 is a workhorse, with a passenger car feel and level of comfort. It even has electric lumbar support for the driver — great when you are spending so much time in the van delivering parcels in the lead-up to Christmas. It certainly has a lot more tech than the diesel he was trading in.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, he was “blown away” by the standard features — the 360-degree camera, for example. “Vans are not known for their visibility.” On his return to the dealership for his first service, he commented on the smoothness of the torque: “It has no issues going uphill.” He reported that the van felt “well planted on the road.” Ray has gotten used to trickle charging at home and has lost his range anxiety. Like most new EV drivers, once he started living and working with the vehicle, his fears vanished. The PV5 supports fast charging also for when Ray needs a boost on the road.

According to recent reports, but what about that all-notable question of cost? Can we make the bean counters happy? The Kia PV5 retails for AU$56,000 (before on-road costs), which is about the same price as comparable diesel vans like the Ford Transit and the Toyota HiAce. Add to that the savings on fuel, the peace of mind from fuel security, and the reduced servicing and it is easy to build a business case for the Kia PV5 — cost per parcel delivery. The PV5 even comes with vehicle to load.

Industry observers note that and it isn’t made in China! Can the PV5 replace Toyota’s HiAce? Find the answer in this video. The reviewer points out many features that make the PV5 an attractive option: the charge port is on the front. The van has lots of nooks and crannies for storage. She measures storage by capacity to fit in bottles of wine — for example, two in the glove box. There is a step provided to alight the van, aided by grab handles. More storage space is provided above the steering wheel, including a nifty phone slot. There are customizable buttons on the steering wheel to create shortcuts; for example, to the air conditioning settings. A wireless phone charger is nestled near the dash. The glovebox contains the V2L adaptor supplied with the van.

Industry observers note that the fact that the van reverts to the lowest regen setting every time you restart the car is a little niggle. That, and there is no frunk — reducing the reviewer’s all-vital need for wine storage. Full specs can be found here. Kia even gives you helpful advice on how to apply for electric vehicle subsidies (last page, bottom right). One of the pictures that caught my eye indicates the PV5 as a flatbed truck.

Recent findings suggest that the PV5 was recently named 2026 International Van of the Year. It measures 4695mm long, 2255mm wide, and 1899mm tall on a 2995mm wheelbase. Range is stated as 416 km, but will of course vary with driving style and load. The battery is a 71.2kWh nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) lithium-ion battery. Kia offers a 165,000 km warranty on the battery. The van is front-wheel drive.

The PV5 has over 4 cubic metres of cargo capacity, double both that of the ID Buzz and the Tesla Model Y. Space enough for two euro pallets. There are multiple access points, with sliding doors on both sides and barn doors in the rear. The rear barn doors open to 180 degrees, and a low 419mm load height improves accessibility.

According to recent reports, goods being shipped are protected by padding on the rear doors and insides of the back. The PV5 can carry up to 740 kg. Tiedowns on the floor of the rear of the van help to secure cargo. There is also a power point in the back of the van. Perhaps a tradie can recharge their tools on site. No frunk for wine.

From the spec sheet: “Standard driver assist features include blind-spot collision avoidance, navigation-based adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane centring with hands-on detection, and parking collision avoidance assist.”.

A launch in the USA is financially difficult because of the 25% “chicken tax.” Kia builds the PV5 in South Korea and classifies it as a commercial vehicle, and it faces a 25% US import tariff on light trucks and commercial vans.

Sources indicate that sadly, the Kia PV5 doesn’t come in red, but only in white, grey and black. Most companies may take up the option of wrapping the van in their own livery. Overall, we were impressed with Kia PV5 and look forward to seeing more of them on the road throughout the suburbs as Australian delivery drivers move towards a bright electric future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The skyward surge in gas prices in 2026 has hit our wallets pretty hard, even more so for those who commute within city limits. And if you use a gas-guzzling sportbike or a heavyweight cruiser to get around town, things are likely even worse for you. Fear not, though, as we've compiled a list of six commuter motorcycles currently on sale (spoiler alert: the overwhelming majority of them are Hondas), all of which claim impressively high fuel efficiency figures — specifically, more than 100 miles per gallon.

Industry observers note that these are manufacturer-claimed figures, of course, but they should still translate to some pretty awesome mileage in the real world, which can help ease your concerns regarding gas prices. What's also great about these motorcycles is that they're very affordably priced. However, don't expect scintillating performance out of them, as they're powered by small-capacity single-cylinder engines. Consequently, these motorcycles are best suited to urban commuting rather than zipping down a highway or freeway. That stated, some of them are dual-sport bikes, which means you can take them to off-road trails on the weekends, if you're into that.

According to recent reports, kicking things off is the WR125R, which, at $3,999 (plus a $400 destination fee), is the most affordable street-legal motorcycle Yamaha offers. The WR125R comes with a 125 cc single-cylinder fuel-injected motor that's liquid-cooled (the only liquid-cooled engine on this list) and develops 14 hp and 8.3 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel through a six-speed wet-clutch gearbox. Yamaha touts an estimated fuel economy of 105 mpg for the WR125R, and the bike features a 2.1-gallon fuel tank, with Yamaha quoting a maximum range of around 200 miles.

Pretty good for a city commuter, right? It doesn't end there, though, as the WR125R is a dual-sport motorcycle. As part of its off-road trappings, the WR125R packs a 41mm (1.6-inch) KYB front fork with 8.5 inches of travel, a linked-type rear Monocross shock with 7.3 inches of travel, and a generous 9.4 inches of ground clearance — all of which can make for a fun ride off the beaten path. At 304 pounds (wet), the WR125R's weight should be easy to manage for rookie riders, though some may find the 34.4-inch seat height on the taller side.

Priced at $2,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the cute Honda Navi is the most affordable motorcycle on this list. The word "motorcycle" does do a bit of heavy lifting here, as the Navi's styling features a dose of scooter influence. Within its chassis sits a 109 cc single-cylinder engine that uses a carburetor, which is simple and easy to repair, but prone to hard starting in colder weather. The engine is also air-cooled instead of liquid-cooled, so it can run hot during long traffic halts.

The Navi makes an estimated 8 hp and 6.5 lb-ft of torque, which is ample for trundling around city blocks at leisurely speeds. Notably, it remains the cheapest new major-brand motorcycle you can buy with an automatic gearbox, specifically a CVT, which furthers the case for the Navi being an ideal city bike. It also weighs just 234 pounds and has a 30-inch seat height, so beginners can get to grips with it quickly. However, Honda has fitted the bike with a teeny-tiny 0.9-gallon fuel tank, so at Honda's claimed 110 mpg, the range works out to around 100 miles. The Navi, therefore, is best suited for those who have short daily commutes.

Like the Yamaha WR125R, the XR150L is Honda's entry-level dual-sport motorcycle, priced at $3,399 (plus a $300 destination fee). It's powered by a 149 cc single-cylinder engine, which is carbureted and air-cooled, and makes 12.6 hp and 9.6 lb-ft of torque. A five-speed manual gearbox transmits that grunt to the rear wheel. As for fuel efficiency, the XR150L is quite a step above the WR125R, and even the smaller-engined Navi. Honda's figures work out to 124 mpg, and the bike offers a 2.8-gallon fuel tank — the largest-capacity tank on this list.

Sources indicate that so, even though the XR150L doesn't tout the highest fuel efficiency here, its relatively major tank enables a claimed range of 346 miles on a single tank. If your commute is on the longer side, this is the motorcycle to go for. Since it's a dual-sport bike, the XR150L additionally features a 31mm (1.22-inch) front fork with 7.1 inches of travel, a single rear shock with 5.9 inches of travel, and 9.6 inches of ground clearance. While the wheel travel is shorter than that offered by the WR125R, the XR150L has more ground clearance, and, at 282 pounds, is a decent bit lighter too. Its seat height is also noticeably lower (32.8 inches), which can make mounting and dismounting easier.

It has been revealed that if you find yourself less interested in dual-sport bikes and motorcycle-scooter hybrids, and lean more toward retro-inspired styling, the Honda Trail125 might just be the bike for you. Priced at $4,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the Trail125 features a distinctive design that draws on Honda's trail-bike heritage, with a high-mounted exhaust, a step-through steel backbone chassis, a rear luggage rack, and spoked wheels. The Trail125 comes fitted with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder engine that's air-cooled and produces 9 hp and 8.1 lb-ft of torque.

According to recent reports, A four-speed semi-automatic transmission — meaning you never have to work a clutch lever — is equipped as standard, and the fuel tank measures 1.4 gallons, which translates to nearly 220 miles between fill-ups, at about 157 mpg. The seat height is 31.5 inches, which is slightly taller than that of the Navi, and the Trail125 weighs 256 pounds, making it heavier than the Navi as well.

Honda's quirkily named Grom is yet another small and cute motorcycle. It's powered by a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder motor that's air-cooled and belts out nearly 10 hp and 7.7 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual gearbox. The Grom is rated for a stellar fuel economy of 161 mpg, and its 1.6-gallon fuel tank means that it can theoretically cover 257 miles before needing a refill.

The Grom is styled much like a downsized conventional motorcycle, so if you're not a fan of the Navi's scooter-like look or the XR150L's dual-sport design, it would likely appeal to you. It also weighs 224 pounds, making it lighter than the Navi, and it even matches the Navi's 30-inch seat height. As for price, the Grom is available in three trim levels, namely the Base ($3,599), SP ($3,699), and ABS ($3,799) — all three carry a destination fee of $300. The Base and SP trims are differentiated by color and graphics (the SP comes solely in a black finish, while the Base trim is offered in red, white, and blue), and the aptly named ABS trim adds front-wheel ABS.

Sources indicate that taking the top spot on this list is the Monkey — one more whimsically named motorcycle from Honda. Much like the Trail125, the Monkey is a retro-inspired motorcycle, but instead of a trail bike, it resembles an old-school scrambler. Pretty cool, right? As for mechanicals, the Monkey comes equipped with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder mill that uses air cooling and develops all of 9 hp and 8 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual transmission.

Industry observers note that despite the Monkey's impressive 163-mpg claimed fuel economy, its 1.5-gallon fuel tank is good for around 244 miles — less than the Grom's. The seat height is also a tiny bit higher at 30.5 inches, and, at 231 pounds, the Monkey is a few pounds heavier than the Grom too. That noted, the Monkey does come with front-wheel ABS as standard. As for the price, the Monkey is available for $4,399 (plus a $300 destination fee), making it the most expensive motorcycle here.

LDEQ issued air permit to the facility despite serious flaws in permit.

Donaldsonville, Louisiana — Today, RISE St. James Louisiana and Sierra Club filed a lawsuit challenging Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality’s decision to glitch an air permit to Hyundai-POSCO for its proposed steelmaking facility. The groups claim that the air permit must be vacated because LDEQ did not conduct an environmental justice analysis, nor did the agency give full and careful consideration to mitigation measures like electrified components and green hydrogen, or to the environmental costs of Hyundai’s added pollution in an already overburdened area, as is required by the Louisiana state constitution and the Clean Air Act.

Recent findings suggest that throughout 2026, Sierra Club, working with other experts and local groups, submitted a series of comments to LDEQ in an effort to bring to light the errors, miscalculations, and omissions in the permit application. Despite some improvements to the permit application, made by Hyundai Steel following public pressure, the final air permit issued by LDEQ authorizes the facility to emit substantial quantities of greenhouse gases, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, lead, mercury, ammonia, and other pollutants. Many of these pollutants cause significant and irreversible damage to human health even at low levels.

The area around the planned facility already bears a toxic air pollution burden greater than 96% of the rest of the country, and ranks high across a range of environmental and socioeconomic indicators. The Hyundai Steel Plant is one of multiple polluting facilities planned as part of the 17,000-acre Riverplex MegaPark in an area known as Cancer Alley in Ascension Parish, Louisiana.

In response, the petitioners issued the following statements:.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Issod, Sierra Club Senior Attorney, remarked: “LDEQ must ensure the Hyundai Steel Plant permit complies with the legal requirements to reduce harmful pollution impacts as much as possible on the surrounding community, which already bears a 96% percentile burden of toxic releases as compared to the national average. By refusing to conduct an environmental justice analysis, consider cleaner technologies like electrifying components and replacing dirty gas with green hydrogen, or consider any environmental costs of Hyundai’s pollution, LDEQ has failed to perform the most basic function of its role and deprived the community of a transparent, thorough, and accurate assessment of the facility’s potential negative impacts. For that reason, we are asking the Court to reverse LDEQ’s final decision and vacate the permit for Hyundai Steel’s proposed facility.”.

Industry observers note that mekaylyn Lavigne, Modeste Coordinator for RISE St. James, mentioned: “I was born and raised in the small and peaceful community of Modeste. Although this region is now known as Cancer Alley because many chemical plants have polluted our air and water, my family and neighbors still enjoy sitting on our porches, watching birds and wildlife, and fishing. Now, LDEQ is allowing a steel mill to move in next door to my home, and tells us the air quality is fine and this massive iron and steel making facility will not have any negative impacts. Modeste residents deserve the truth. The court should make LDEQ go back to the drawing board on this permit to disclose all the impacts and use the cleanest technologies to reduce pollution.”.
