Sources indicate that crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

Recent findings suggest that the current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

Sources indicate that that monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

This time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

Recent findings suggest that A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

Industry News: Drought-Stricken Nevada Town Erupts Over Luxury Development’s Plan for ‘Firefighter Pond’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region?
  • That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.
  • Industry observers note that joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region? What if that developer notes that firefighters can access the pond to fight wildfires?

That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.

Industry observers note that joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness. The Reserve is being built on 65 acres that were once home to the Bonnie Springs Ranch, a historic, Old West-themed family resort that once featured horseback riding and a small zoo.

Two-acre empty plots in the community start at $7.5 million. But that’s not what has the community up in arms. Instead, it’s what the Reserve is touting on its website: a large human-made pond in the middle of the property.

Sources indicate that to outsiders, it seems like just one feature in a long list of amenities. But for some locals in Clark County, which was declared a natural disaster area due to drought earlier this year, the pond seems like a slap in the face—even as the developers attempt to position it as a fire safety "dip pond.".

“This little dip pond here is really fire safety as an afterthought, and I think that’s pretty obvious in terms of even their planning,” stated Sarah J. McCrea-Dameron, a Blue Diamond, NV, resident and former deputy fire chief from Las Vegas Fire & Rescue, at a zoning commission meeting this past week. “It’s not in an area that’s necessary, and it’s not the best use of that water and that precious resource for our community.“.

The Reserve at Red Rock Canyon development sits within the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area, an expansive 195,000-acre area within the Mojave Desert. Aztec sandstone foundations dating back to 180 million years can be found in the area, along with sea fossils and hundreds of local bird species. More than 3 million people visit the area each year.

According to recent reports, water for the area is supplied by the Colorado River. In recent years, the river and the several lakes it feeds have been pushed to the limit, as latest development, coupled with more frequent droughts, have strained resources.

The river doesn’t just supply necessary water to communities across the Southwest: It also produces much-needed hydropower for the region.

Earlier this year, Lake Powell, one of the lakes fed by the Colorado River, dropped to its lowest level in history, threatening to shut down the Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies power to Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Latest Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Nebraska.

Recent findings suggest that communities around the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area take the mantle of water conservation seriously. In fact, in 2020, the nearby community of Blue Diamond issued a temporary moratorium on “the issuance of additional water commitments” that remains in place.

Now, as the developers Laub and Jones offer unbuilt lots in their upcoming development for $7.5 million, they are pitching the proposed pond as a neighborhood amenity.

“Paths and roads will meander past water features fed by the canyon’s natural springs,” the development’s website states.

Recent findings suggest that but those types of features are typically prohibited by Clark County’s Title 30, which governs building and development in the area. Title 30 right now prohibits the creation of human-made lakes of any size and water features greater than 10 square feet of surface area. So the developers stressed that the human-made pond would be fed via private water rights, and therefore not impede on community resources. Instead of using Colorado River resources, the project would be fed using groundwater.

Bob Gronauer, the developers' lawyer, remarked the water feature would be a “dip pond”—a water source for use by firefighting helicopters. Wildfires are a frequent problem in the region. In 2025 alone, there were 619 fires in the state, which destroyed more than 368,000 acres.

Industry observers note that in fact, the developers have already signed a use agreement with the Nevada Division of Forestry. The developers claimed the NDF came to them to ask them to create the pond, but the NDF stated the developers approached them about the partnership, the Nevada Independent reported.

"We reached out to the Bureau of Land Management Red Rock management staff at the visitor center, Save Red Rock, Friends of Red Rock, as well as the Nature Conservancy Nevada immediately upon purchasing the property to work with them to make this development compatible with the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area," Laub tells Realtor.com. (Laub is the chairman of the Nature Conservancy board.).

Laub says the idea for the dip pond actually came from the BLM.

It has been revealed that "They asked if we could work with them on fire management in Red Rock Canyon, and would we consider providing water for firefighting. Of course our answer was yes. We have a 220,000-gallon water tank designed into our water system for supplying water to our fire hydrants, and we agreed to provide a fire hydrant for the BLM water tankers to fill up in the event of a wildfire," Laub continues.

"The ponds are designed to fit into the canyon ecosystem and look natural but also to be compatible with helicopter firefighting.".

Laub tells Realtor.com that they've already been testing the wells in the canyon, and "none of the testing results from these wells has indicated a draw down of significance from our use of the water system.".

He also notes that they purchased the water rights from Bonnie Springs Ranch, which had been in use for more than 60 years.

"The property has had ponds, streams, pools, and springs from the original ranch in 1952," he explains.

To expedite the creation of the dip pools, the developers proposed an amendment to Title 30 that would add language permitting “a body of water, served from standalone private water rights, within 1,000 feet of a National Conservation Area, intended for fire suppression and life safety purposes as agreed upon with a State or Federal Agency.”In October, Clark County Planning Commission's professional staff recommended denying the amendment.

In a recent development, "As proposed, there is no indication of how these water features would be designed, the capacity of these water features, or other potential uses for the stored water. The proliferation of non-essential water features will place an additional burden on the existing water supply," the staff recommendation read. "Furthermore, this request may encourage additional non-essential water features within residential and nonresidential development.".

In a recent development, however, the Planning Commission approved the amendment by a vote of 6-1. It then went to the Clark County Zoning Board for approval. On Wednesday night, during the public comment period of the meeting, around a dozen community members spoke out against the planned feature.

“You can design a decorative water feature and then call it a dip pond. You can offer to let the Forest Service use it knowing that they never will because of the way it’s designed and location, but that doesn’t make that decorative water feature a piece of critical fire infrastructure," noted former Clark County Fire Capt. Erik Klausen.

“They’re trying to put a plastic fire helmet on this water feature and tell us it’s about public safety,” he continued.

At the end of the public comment period, all seven commissioners voted in favor of the proposed amendment, though, as Commissioner Justin Jones noted, the approval of the amendment does not mean the dip pond project has been approved.

Furthermore, noted Commissioner Marilyn Kirkpatrick, the project needs to be fit for purpose.

"If it's a fire-suppression pond, then it has to be a fire-suppression pond in my mind," said Kirkpatrick. "It should stay as a fire-supression pond, not as a recreational venue, not as irrigation, because that water is supposed to be there for a reason.".

Realtor.com has reached out to developer Jones and lawyer Gronauer for comment.

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.
  • Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations.
  • That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA proposal Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth remarked in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage prepares and listed on the Medicare proposal finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the manufacturer stated that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

According to recent reports, "Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the manufacturer noted.

Sources indicate that in addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the tech giant mentioned.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the looks available to them," Elevance said.

Recent findings suggest that "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the organization continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans.".

UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer mentioned that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in intends with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

Recent findings suggest that the use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the firm, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in looks with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company remarked in the lawsuit.

Industry observers note that CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 strategy year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene stated.

"Beyond the financial impact to the manufacturer and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company stated in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Sources indicate that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer indicates that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The manufacturer argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to proposal payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment stated in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

Industry observers note that CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

According to recent reports, "Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about blueprint enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the manufacturer said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

According to recent reports, in addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, remarked that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment mentioned in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the manufacturer noted.

Latest Update: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed.
  • Recent findings suggest that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests.
  • The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an vital step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Recent findings suggest that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging.

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

Industry observers note that however, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

Industry observers note that "That put me on a different path," mentioned Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work.".

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

Newly introduced DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work.

According to recent reports, sehgal is the lead author of the latest study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," noted Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions.".

It has been revealed that biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

How Scientists Measure Biological Age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

It has been revealed that these tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

Sources indicate that the researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

It has been revealed that across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

In a recent development, "What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers.".

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Indicated the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

According to recent reports, one of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.).

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months.".

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

In a recent development, "We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood.".

Key Questions About Slowing Aging Remain.

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen mentioned.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:.

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures revealed little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

Lawmakers form bipartisan caucus to create meaningful AI safety legislation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers mentioned today they’re forming a fresh AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.
  • Recent findings suggest that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:48 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers mentioned today they’re forming a fresh AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

Recent findings suggest that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

These incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” mentioned Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”.

Whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

Industry observers note that does it feel like there's a fresh tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6.

— Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026.

According to recent reports, the 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides said the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding promptly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

Industry observers note that “We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He said the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse upcoming AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety issues, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to latest legislation and debate.

According to recent reports, in the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major glitch for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

It has been revealed that “Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue,” Moran said. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”.
